guest.bio_context: Dino Cardelli brings over 35 years of hands-on expertise across grower, processor, and C-suite roles in the juice ingredients and agronomic sectors. He has worked for major global companies including Sun Orchard Juicery, PepsiCo, The Coca-Cola Company, Tropicana, and Dole. He has lived, worked, and managed projects in over 50 countries, speaks fluent Spanish, and has led strategic, operational, tactical, and indirect procurement initiatives across the entire global value chain. He spoke at the World Juice Summit in Antwerp in 2023 on the intersection of supply chain and technical operations in the post-pandemic environment.

pending_qa.q: What is the difference between a mentality required for fresh produce procurement versus juice procurement?
pending_qa.r: A juice procurement professional must monitor geopolitical events and global weather patterns differently than fresh buyers. When tropical storms form in the Gulf, juice procurement teams think about where the storm will track and whether it will hit the citrus belt. An earthquake in the Kalima area triggers immediate supplier outreach to assess impact. This global, proactive risk-management mindset differs fundamentally from fresh market thinking.

pending_qa.q: How has consolidation in citrus growing and juice processing regions reshaped supply chain complexity?
pending_qa.r: Over the past 15-20 years, the industry has consolidated dramatically. Where there used to be eight to ten different growers in a region, now there are two or three. Similarly, the Mexican juice processing industry went from many small processors to three or four major ones. In the Colima area and along the coast, three or four large consolidated players now dominate, which changes how procurement teams must negotiate and plan supply.

pending_qa.q: What role did triwall bins play in improving juice fruit quality and storage efficiency in procurement?
pending_qa.r: Dino and Patrick were among the first to introduce triwall bins for juice fruit instead of traditional gondolas. Triwalls could be stored in cold rooms, which meant that when trailers or gondolas were unavailable, teams could retrieve triwalls from the warehouse and dump the fruit. This approach maintained consistent fruit quality and gave procurement teams flexibility in managing logistics—plus they achieved rejection rates of less than 1% because they were able to control conditions and inspect loads in person.

pending_qa.q: How did yield-based pricing models align supplier incentives with juice quality specifications?
pending_qa.r: Dino created spreadsheets that tied price to yield: if a supplier could guarantee higher gallons-per-ton output, they could earn a premium price. This incentivized growers to send the best quality fruit, because better fruit meant higher juice yields and higher revenue for both parties. The model worked so well with triwalls because both parties could control and measure the actual yield outcomes.

pending_qa.q: What does modern citrus procurement knowledge require that technology and spreadsheets alone cannot provide?
pending_qa.r: Education and deep understanding of global production regions are essential. In today's world with accessibility to everything, teams often rely only on technology and spreadsheets to tell them what to buy, at what price and size, without understanding the 'why' behind those specifications. Dino emphasizes that procurement professionals need foundational knowledge about each region's identity, geopolitical risks, seasonal dynamics, and agronomic factors to make strategic decisions beyond transactional purchasing.
